The HOLDOUT verdict is clear: **E5 doesn't replicate**. The pooled gain is -0.40 ± 0.98 on 1,000 problems (46 gained, 50 lost). The flip itself worked as designed: 354 answers moved Here→Let and none went the other way. But its predicted benefit was absent, with the flipped group at -0.56 ± 2.30 against +5.81 ± 2.85 on DEV, while cut-offs in that group rose from 22.9% to 30.8%. So the DEV gain was mostly noise or selection, even though those sets were fresh for E5. I'd read the mechanism as "Let raises looping about as much as it raises quality". The all-data figure of +0.65 ± 0.70 is context only, and it doesn't change the decision. `/work/edited` is empty, so the original is the current submission.

18 passes remain, and any new candidate would need to clear the same bar. The lesson for sizing is that a 1-2 point DEV gain can't be trusted, so I need effects well above that. Among the open ideas, the E11 dose curve is the most concrete. Sharpening cost words (-0.35 ± 0.10) and earlier-result recall (-1.50 ± 0.49). If those effects are monotonic rather than a peak at the natural setting, flattening head 0 should improve exactly those token classes, and words carry the planning decisions.

So E11b scales the 44 near-dead rows of head 0 up by 1.567 instead of zeroing them. That uses more of the RMS budget and should lower the head's temperature to about 0.8x, with almost no change in direction. A positive word and earlier-recall shift of at least 2 standard errors would be real news, justifying a generation test. A negative or flat shift means the natural temperature is already near its best, and I'd close attention sharpness at two strengths.

E11b is saved. The estimated temperature is 0.80x, the dead dimensions still carry only 0.28% of logit energy, and the notes are up to date. This pass uses the same 1,024 texts as passes 7 and 28, so I can read the two strengths on either side of the natural setting directly. The continue rule was fixed before the pass: word and earlier-recall accuracy must each rise by at least 2 standard errors, with no class falling.

The summary's per-text logprobs look a little higher than in the sharpening pass, but the class comparison is what counts. I'll run the same table against pass 7 and apply the rule I fixed beforehand: words and earlier recall up by at least 2 standard errors, and no class down. The overall logprob change will show whether the dose curve passes through the natural setting or peaks there.

Flattening also loses, and this time clearly on accuracy: `fromproblem_first` -1.90 ± 0.42, `fromproblem_later` -0.76 ± 0.22, words -0.23 ± 0.07, and arithmetic overall -0.46 ± 0.21. My continue rule is failed in both directions, and there's no reversal to exploit. The two strengths together do give a clean causal result. Lowering head 0's sharpness damages retrieval, so the head really does contribute, while raising it adds nothing. The natural setting is already at the plateau, so I'm closing attention sharpness at L17 head 0.

Across all the work so far, a pattern stands out: retrieval, operand reading and register selection all sit close to their best settings. What I never examined at component level is the most visible failure, the 26% of answers cut off in loops. HOLDOUT shows this directly: E5's Let answers looped more, which cancelled any quality gain. I closed loop breaking based on neuron contrasts, which found nothing isolated, and on stopping at onset, which rarely gave gold. I never asked whether a specific attention head does the copying. Stopping a loop and preventing one are also different: a model that can't copy its last line might go on reasoning.

So the next step is one attention pass on real loops, original model, with no edits active. Two texts of up to 2,048 tokens can each hold two cut Let answers, giving four loops. For each full-attention head I'll measure how much attention lands exactly one period back on the copied tokens, against the same lag before the loop starts. A head that locks onto the copy position would be a real candidate to weaken in generation. If attention is spread across heads, there's no single copy circuit here and I'll close the line for good. This block picks the answers and builds the texts.
